manifest.name: dsh-mcp-mcp-status
manifest.description: MCP server inventory for the dsh Web Settings dialog: every configured MCP server with its status, transport, target, tool count, and enablement

scripts.build: tsc -b tsconfig.host.json && tsdown --config tsdown.config.ts && tsc -b tsconfig.client.json && tsdown --config tsdown.client.config.ts
scripts.prepare: tsc -b tsconfig.host.json && tsdown --config tsdown.config.ts && tsc -b tsconfig.client.json && tsdown --config tsdown.client.config.ts
scripts.clean: node --eval "for (const p of ['packages/status/lib']) require('node:fs').rmSync(p, { recursive: true, force: true })"

bundle.text:
# Patch layer for dsh-mcp-mcp-status, declared by `dsh.bundle.patch` and applied
# when a profile lists `dsh-mcp-mcp-status` in `dsh.profile.bundles`.
#
# One row is the whole plugin. A row whose package declares `dsh.client` is
# simultaneously a Host row and a browser roster row: the modules node half
# scans Loader entries for packages declaring `dsh.client` and registers that
# package's `./client` export under the row's package name. The inserted row
# therefore mounts the `mcpInventory` service and the Settings section together.
#
# The row is inserted rather than id-targeted because an id patch cannot point
# an existing row at a different package: a patch `name` asserts the target's
# plugin name instead of renaming it, and a patch that matches no row is
# skipped with a warning. Nothing is disabled: current DSH releases ship no
# in-tree MCP inventory, so this row is the only provider of that service.
- insert:
    - id: mcp-status
      name: dsh-mcp-mcp-status

readme.text: An installable DeepSeek Harness plugin that adds an **MCP** section to the Web Settings dialog, listing every MCP server the active profile configures with its derived status, transport, target, registered tools, and an enable/disable switch.

The package replaces the MCP inventory earlier DSH releases shipped in-tree (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-host-mcp-inventory` and `@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-ui-settings-mcp`) as one dual-face package: the package root is the Host side (`mcpInventory` service) and the `./client` export is the browser side (the Settings section). It reads only published surfaces — the Loader and the tool registry — so no DSH release has to carry an inventory-publication seam for it to work.

The Settings section lists one row per configured MCP server: the server name from the entry's config (falling back to the Loader entry id), a status tag, the transport and connection target from that stored config, the tools registered under the server's namespace, and a switch. Its navigation row draws the package's own glyph — a server node above two tool nodes — through the shell's `settings.section.icon` slot instead of the shell's fallback icon.

The status is derived from the Loader entry and the tool registry: `disabled` for a row the profile has switched off, which is still listed because the configured set comes from the Loader rather than from a connection; `failed` when the entry's Loader fiber is in its failed phase; `connected` once the server has registered at least one tool under its `mcp__<serverName>__` namespace; and `starting` in every remaining case.

Two situations are indistinguishable in that derivation: a server that is negotiating or retrying reports `starting`, exactly like one that has not started yet, and a connected server that registers no tool reports `starting` as well. The text of the last connection failure is not exposed by any of these surfaces, so the section no longer renders it.

The switch persists one server's enablement in the current profile through the profile manager and returns the re-read inventory; when the Host has no profile manager composed, `managementAvailable` is false and the section renders the switches inert rather than pretending the write would work.

Nothing here is model-visible: the Host service reads the Loader configuration and the tool registry, and the section reads that service. No prompt, tool schema, or session log entry is involved.

Substitute your GitHub owner for `<user>`; the repository must be named `dsh-mcp-mcp-status` so the installed package name matches the profile's dependency key (rename the repository and pnpm derives a different key, which then needs an alias such as `dsh-mcp-mcp-status@github:<user>/other-name`).

```sh
dsh plugin --profile demo add github:<user>/dsh-mcp-mcp-status
```

The first run fails: pnpm ≥ 10 refuses to run the `prepare` script that builds the git checkout, and `dsh` prints the exact blocked key and the file to edit.

Add that key to the profile's `pnpm-workspace.yaml` — `~/.dsh/profiles/demo/pnpm-workspace.yaml` by default — then run the same command again:

```yaml
allowBuilds:
  dsh-mcp-mcp-status: true
```

`pnpm-workspace.yaml` is where pnpm ≥ 10 reads its settings, not `.npmrc`, and the key must match the blocked package exactly; a version-qualified key that a different pnpm release prints is equally valid. A prebuilt tarball or a local checkout installed by path needs no allowance, because neither runs the `prepare` script.
Restart the server after a bundle-list edit; client bundles are served from `lib/`, so a browser refresh alone does not pick up a rebuilt plugin.

The patch inserts one row and disables nothing, so this package registers both the `mcpInventory` Host service and the Settings section on its own. Current DSH releases ship no in-tree MCP inventory, so no other row provides that service or renders that section.

A composition may still provide the namespace — an older `@deepseek-ai/dsh-host-mcp-inventory` mounted by the Web app's own Client assembly (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-api-remotes`), or another plugin. The Gateway rejects a second contribution for one namespace, so the browser half reads it first — a non-strict `ctx.get('remote.mcpInventory')` — and mounts its own generated contribution only when nothing provides it. The descriptors address the namespace by method name, so an existing contribution dispatches to this package's Host service either way, and the plugin withdraws only what it added.

The bundle list above is what makes the patch layer apply: with `dsh-mcp-mcp-status` absent from `dsh.profile.bundles`, the plugin's row is never inserted, and removing the package from the list removes the section again.
The Host side is a Cordis service registered under the key `mcpInventory` (readable as `ctx.mcpInventory`) and projected to the browser as the Remote namespace `remote.mcpInventory`.

| Remote method | Signature | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `list` | `() => Promise<McpInventorySnapshot>` | Every Loader entry naming `@deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-client`, in Loader order, each with the status and tools derived from that entry and the registry. |
| `setEnabled` | `(entryId: PluginEntryId, enabled: boolean) => Promise<McpInventorySnapshot>` | Persists one entry's enablement through the profile manager and returns the re-read inventory. Rejects when no profile manager is composed, when the manager refuses the target as read-only, or when the value was already in the requested state. |

`McpServerInfo` carries `entryId`, `serverName`, `transport` (`stdio`, `streamable-http`, or `unknown`), an optional `target`, `enabled`, `status`, `tools`, and an optional `readOnlyReason`. `McpInventorySnapshot` adds `managementAvailable`.

A row's identity, transport, and target come from the entry's stored config, and its tools are the model-facing names the tool registry holds in the `mcp__<serverName>__` namespace, so a tool the server registers later appears on the next read with no publication step in between.

`prepare` runs the same four steps that `build` runs, in this order: `tsc -b tsconfig.host.json` emits the Host types and JavaScript into `packages/status/lib/types`, `tsdown --config tsdown.config.ts` bundles the Host half into `packages/status/lib/index.js` and lets the Typert generator emit the face artifacts beside it, `tsc -b tsconfig.client.json` emits the browser half, and `tsdown --config tsdown.client.config.ts` bundles it into the closure-factory artifact `packages/status/lib/client.js`.

The Typert generator's real input contract is the reason for the file layout at the repository root. Its tsdown plugin resolves the workspace anchor by walking up from the build's output directory until it finds a `tsconfig.host.json`, so the root must own that file and `packages/status` must not contain one — a file of that name inside the package directory would move the anchor and silently stop artifact generation. From the anchor it reads the aggregate's project references, and it accepts only packages physically under `<anchor>/packages`, which is why the build project lives at `packages/status` rather than beside the root manifest. Each accepted registration must declare a `./typert` export, and the emitted artifacts are written into that package's own `lib/`. Only those registrations are emitted for, but they are not the only packages the analysis recognizes: a declaration resolved from `node_modules` belongs to the installed package named by its nearest ancestor `package.json`, so the protocol's `@Remote` and `TypertRemoteService` decorators and the Remote boundary types this package imports from published dependencies count as published surfaces rather than as unowned decl

The browser artifact calls `window.__ModuleLoader__.load({ id: 'dsh-mcp-mcp-status', factory })` and resolves externals through the `require` the loader hands to the factory. The id equals the package name, which is exactly the key the client module registry uses for the row, and only the shell's static module table stays external — `zod` and the generated Remote contribution are inlined, because a `require` the module table cannot answer throws when the factory materializes.

`tsdown.client.ts` is a standalone replacement for the monorepo's repository-internal `packages/client/tsdown.client.ts`. It keeps the artifact rules — closure-factory wrapper, baseline externals, lightningcss-compiled CSS Modules injecting one tagged `style` per stylesheet, and source maps chained back through the `.tsx` sources — and drops the monorepo's repository-level gates: the bundle-input isolation check, the client bundle purity allowlist (it names other monorepo packages), the async-chunk `require.async` rewrite (this package has no dynamic chunks), and the `?inline`/global stylesheet loaders (this package ships only a `.module.css`).

The Host half imports only published surfaces: `@deepseek-ai/cordis-plugin-loader` for the Loader entries, `@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools` for the tool registry, and `@deepseek-ai/dsh-typert-protocol` for the Remote decorators. No DSH release has to export a publication seam for it, and `tsc -b tsconfig.host.json` compiles the half against the published `0.2.0-rc.2`.

The consequence is concrete: with the seam gone, nothing in the build or at runtime waits for a release that carries one, and the published `0.2.0-rc.2` packages satisfy every import this package makes — the Loader's entry list and fiber state and the registry's `schemas()` are public members of the published surfaces.

Every `@deepseek-ai/dsh-*` dependency and peer is `^0.2.0-rc.2`; `@deepseek-ai/cordis` is `~4.0.4` and `@deepseek-ai/cordis-plugin-loader` is `~1.0.5`, both being published on their own version lines rather than the DSH line.

The ported unit tests are not included. They were written against `@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-test-runtime`, which is not published, so the browser suites cannot resolve their runtime; `vitest` and `@testing-library/react` would add a test-only dependency tree to a package whose whole job is a build-time `prepare`.

The browser baseline in `tsdown.client.ts` is a copy of the shell's static module table (`PLATFORM_MODULES` plus the empty `PRELOADED_CLIENT_EXTERNALS`). A row added to the shell's table after this file was written is not requested by this package, so it would be inlined here instead of shared; that is a duplicated module identity, not a load failure, and it is fixed by adding the specifier to the copy.

No run against a live profile was possible in the port environment: no `dsh web` observation covers the row, the patch layering, the namespace reuse, or the Settings rendering, so those are documented from the source they were ported from. The build does complete with a Typert generator that recognizes installed package owners: the Host bundle emits `packages/status/lib/typert.host.*` and `packages/status/lib/typert.remote-client.*`, and both `tsc -b tsconfig.host.json` and `tsc -b tsconfig.client.json` exit 0. Without that recognition the generator fails the Host bundle step with `typert(host): dsh-mcp-mcp-status publishes Remote artifacts but has no Remote methods`, and the browser half then cannot resolve the `dsh-mcp-mcp-status/remote` artifact that step emits. Building this package from npm alone therefore waits on a `@deepseek-ai/dsh-typert-generator` release carrying that recognition.

`README.i18n.yaml` is intentionally absent. The bilingual pairing record next to a translated README is generated by the harness repository's own `verify-translation-pairing --write` step, which does not exist in this standalone repository; hand-writing its per-heading digests would record values nothing verified.
